chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
title: European audiences, dancing and women, and constant touring at home
summary: Audiences in Europe reacted as in America to the band's book, and Crawford says the band toured every whistle stop at home.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: He just didn't play the bands too well.
But, so not like, what were the -- how did the -- did the audiences give you a different feeling in Europe than they did in America?

No. No, they didn't, even in the Scandinavian countries, where they perhaps are used to doing the polka and all those kind of dances, we played just what we went there to play, and we played it, and we went over quite well.
What kind of dances did they do? Did they do American dances to music or --
Yeah, they all copy after American style of dancing. We didn't play no lot of sambas, rhumbas and things like that. We just played our book. Yeah, we went over quite well.
What was the -- you know how like in the music business a lot of times there are women who chase after musicians [because] --

They're over there too. But we didn't pay much attention to that. Of course, we all loved women because we were young fellows, '37, 1937. We only stayed over there -- I can't recall, maybe eight months, six months or a year. I don't remember.
Oh, you stayed over there at least six months, though, huh?

Yeah, traveling, different cities. In this country here, America, I don't think we missed a whistle stop in this country, from Maine to Florida, from New York to California, over and over again, over and over and over.
